summary:
The Prove It Act of 2024 amends the Regulatory Flexibility Act, chapter 6 of title 5, United States Code, to expand small-entity impact analysis, create a petition-based review process for agency certifications that proposed rules lack significant small-entity impacts, require publication of guidance for certain rules, and impose consequences for failure to conduct required 10-year retrospective reviews.

Section 2 amends 5 U.S.C. 603(b) to require an initial regulatory flexibility analysis, where feasible, to describe reasonably foreseeable potential indirect costs imposed on small entities, including entities transacting with directly regulated entities, entities regulated by other governmental entities as a result of the rule, and entities not directly regulated by the agency but otherwise subject to other agency rules as a result of the rule. It amends 5 U.S.C. 605(b) to require an agency, not later than 10 days after completing a certification that a proposed rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities, to publish the certification as provided in that subsection.

Section 2 also adds 5 U.S.C. 605A. New section 605A authorizes any small entity, group of small entities, or organization representing small-entity interests to petition the Chief Counsel for Advocacy of the Small Business Administration to review a 5 U.S.C. 605(b) certification. The Chief Counsel must prescribe and post petition and consultation procedures. Petitions must include specified identifying information, alleged defects in the certification, supporting nonprotected or nonconfidential data, proposed solutions, and supporting analysis. The Chief Counsel must conduct an initial prima facie review and, within 10 days after receipt, either close the matter or notify the petitioner and agency that a full review will occur. A full review must consider affected small entities, adequacy of economic data, and economic implications, and must include a meeting with the petitioner, agency representatives, and the Administrator of the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs. Results must be submitted and published within 30 days after the full review begins. If the Chief Counsel determines the rule would have the requisite significant impact, the agency must prepare initial and final regulatory flexibility analyses under 5 U.S.C. 603 and 604. If the agency fails to attend the meeting or otherwise assist, the final rule shall not apply to small entities. For chapter 7 judicial review, the certification becomes final agency action upon the Chief Counsel’s no-further-review determination or publication of full-review results.

Section 3 amends 5 U.S.C. 609 to require agencies, for rules likely to have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities, to publish on regulations.gov or a similar website all guidance and other relevant documents, including updated interpretive guidance, and allow comments.

Section 4 amends 5 U.S.C. 610 to add indirect costs to periodic review factors. It further provides that if an agency fails to complete a required section 610 review within the 10-year period, the Chief Counsel shall notify the agency that the rule has ceased to be effective; the agency must publish notice and solicit reinstatement comments; and, if the agency determines reinstatement is warranted, it has 180 days to complete the review, after which the rule is reinstated without 5 U.S.C. 553 notice-and-comment procedures. This cessation-and-reinstatement provision applies to final rules issued during the five years preceding enactment or on or after enactment. The Act contains no authorization of appropriations or direct appropriation.
